units: one of the two cloths comes from the fleece clipped off a farmed animal
the other cloth is drawn from a plant after soaking and crushing

text: Lay two lengths of cloth side by side on a workbench and they tell opposite stories. One begins as a fleece clipped from a grazing animal, and its crimped fibres trap pockets of air that hold warmth against the skin. The other is drawn from a plant stem, soaked until it loosens, then crushed and combed into a smooth thread, cool under the fingers. The weaver builds on that contrast. The animal fibre goes into cold-weather clothing, where a thick weave slows the escape of heat. The plant fibre goes into shirts, since it carries damp away from the body. Care pulls the two apart again. Hot water makes the animal fibre tighten and mat together, while the plant cloth survives washing after washing yet creases at the slightest fold. Choosing a cloth, then, means choosing a climate as much as a way of looking after it.

text: My neighbour, who sews for a living, opened up her workroom to me one wet evening, and I came away quite sure that I knew nothing at all about the clothes on my back. She started with her cloth, stacked by kind: the soft cottons, the coarse weaves that scratch the palm, the fine knits that ladder the moment a pin catches them. Then came the tools of the trade, a dented thimble, a pair of scissors nobody else may touch, a flat stick of chalk for marking lines. After that she showed me her hands at work, and there I lost the thread for good, because she builds a cuff, drops in a lining, turns a collar, and never measures twice. Last of all she talked about her customers, who bring back cheap jackets that gape at the shoulder. She laughs about them, then picks up the needle and rescues the thing.

units: the first step is to wear the trousers in front of a mirror

text: Taking up a pair of trousers that hang far too long is a matter of order rather than of skill, and the alteration shops all set out the very same run of steps. Put the trousers on and stand in front of a mirror, fold the cloth to the height you want, and mark that line with pins set close together. Slip them off again, undo the original hem with an unpicker, and then press the fold flat so that the old crease stops showing. Cutting comes next, and here you leave a margin of cloth below the marked line, since without it nothing can be put back. Turn the surplus inwards, pin it, and join it with a stitch that never shows on the outer face. A last pass of the iron settles and flattens the edge. Those who do this for a living advise trying the garment on before any pin comes out.

text: The mill had stood idle at the foot of the valley, and now its looms are beating again. Behind the change lies a quiet shift in taste. Buyers grew tired of knitwear that bobbles after a few washes, and began asking for longer, harder-twisted yarn, whatever the extra cost. That demand gave the fleeces of the surrounding farms a market price once more, where the breeders had been burning them for want of anyone to buy. From there the effect spread outward. Carding sheds reopened, a dye house lit its vats again, and workrooms relearned how to set a neckline by hand. The technical manager puts it plainly: the weave of a jumper tells you how a whole district is faring. One shadow remains, since trained hands are scarce and the learning asks for a patience few applicants will offer.

units: the work garment described takes greater strain than an office one

text: A site jacket takes punishment that office clothing never meets. At the shoulder the armhole opens and shuts from first light until dusk, and the seam there gives way before anything else. At the pockets the weight of tools drags the cloth down and pulls the front out of shape. At the elbows, rubbing against rough surfaces wears the weave through to a hole. Makers answer each of these in turn. They cut the armhole wider and set a triangular gusset beneath it, so the sleeve follows the arm. They back every pocket and lock its corners with extra stitching. On the elbow they lay a patch of heavy canvas that can be swapped without taking the sleeve apart. The lining, meanwhile, unclips and comes away once the cold season ends, which stretches the life of the jacket further.

text: Let us set two wardrobes against each other. The first holds a modest number of garments chosen slowly, several of them past their tenth year and carrying mends that anyone at all can see. The second is crammed with things bought on impulse, worn for a season, then dropped because the knit had gone slack or a buttonhole had torn at the first snag. The gap is usually blamed on money. What one actually observes says otherwise, for the owner of the crowded wardrobe has spent the larger sum. What divides the two habits is attention paid to how a thing is made. Look at a seam, tug at a loose thread, turn back a collar to judge the lining: such checks cost nothing and rule out whatever is doomed from the start. We ought to be teaching them just as we teach people to read a food label.

text: The woman who alters clothes for a living works out of a narrow room at the back of a shopping arcade, and her trade falls into three parts. First come the accidents put right: a tear at the knee, a buttonhole stretched out of shape, a hem ripped away by the heel of a shoe. Then comes fitting to the body, which fills the greater part of her week, since a standard size matches almost no real figure. She takes in a back, tightens a neckline gone slack, shortens a sleeve by no more than the width of a fingernail. Last comes conversion, the part she likes best, when a dated dress becomes a skirt and a worn coat gives up its lining to another. She learned the whole craft beside an elderly tailor, then spent two decades refining it alone. An apprentice in a hurry she turns away.

text: Honestly, that coat had me doubting it from the very start. Right through the first cold season the collar kept riding up, the gathers at the back puffed out oddly, and the colour looked drab beside my old jacket. By the second season the cloth had softened and had taken on the shape of my shoulders, and the lapels began to sit flat without my touching them. The third season was the best of the lot, since it rained without a break, and the surface drank the water and dried overnight, with no smell left behind. Then the lining split under the arm, and I gave the coat up for lost altogether. A repair cost a tenth of what I paid for it, and off it went for another round. My verdict: buy it, provided you accept that it looks awful to begin with. It wears better than I do myself.

text: Dear sister, I am writing before the crate leaves, because what is packed inside it needs a word of explanation. You will be receiving our father's blue jacket. I am not sending it out of sentiment, but because the damp up under the roof had already begun to eat at the lining, and a garment left lying in a trunk ends up as food for moths. The outer cloth has not suffered at all, and that is what decided me to save it. You will notice that the right cuff is frayed, worn thin where his arm rested on the bench and polished the weave away. A seamstress here assures me that a piece taken from under the collar would leave the mend invisible. Have the work done, and then wear it without any worry. Cloth of that kind stiffens while it sleeps and softens once it is out on a back.

units: the text deals with the insect that damages woollen knitwear

text: Ought we to fear the insect that riddles our woollens? The question comes round at the close of every cold season, at the moment when the knitwear is put away. It is not the winged adult that eats the mesh, but its larva, blind and tiny, drawn to animal fibre and above all to the traces of sweat soaked into it. Hence the first of the answers: a clean garment makes poor feeding. What of the storing itself? A closed, opaque cover beats an open shelf, and two nights in the cold kills any eggs laid in a seam. And the old remedies, those scented sachets tucked between the piles? They drive the creature off without killing it, and their strength fades fast. The lasting answer is a dull habit, namely taking the woollens out, shaking them, airing them, and folding them a different way.
